## EXISTING 

This pipeline was used for progress report 2, it has been updated to reflect the final analysis

## Prereqs

In addition to tidyverse packages, `corrplot`, `mda.biber`, `spacyr`, `udpipe`, and `quanteda` will all need to be installed. 

Additionally, an installation of python (3.10+). Once these are installed, everything can be completed within R as described below. 

[Information on spaCy](https://spacy.io/usage)

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(corrplot)
library(lme4)
library(mda.biber)
library(spacyr)
library(quanteda)
library(udpipe)
library(pseudobibeR)
```

## Intro

This pipeline describes the process of completing the MDA. See the [Santa Barbara Pipeline](santa_barbara_pipeline.md) and the [Scraps from the Loft Pipeline](scraps_from_loft_pipeline.md) for information on how the component data frames were assembled and where the data came from. 

This document is used to describe how the individual data frames were combined, the shape of the resulting data frame, and the steps of the analysis. If more details are needed to explain the steps of the MDA, see the [MDA document](mda.md). Final results and exploration of the analysis is documented in the [Dramaticity Analysis](final_report.md) document. 

## Creating all_transcripts df

First, we load in the tv_show_transcripts pipeline as a csv (saved to avoid repeated webscraping).

```{r}
#| output: false

tv_show_df <- read.csv("private/tv_show_transcripts.csv")

tv_show_df
```


Then, we can load in the SB data frame. 

```{r}
#| output: false

sb_files <- read.csv("private/sb_files.csv")

sb_files
```


Finally, we combine the two data frames.

```{r}
#| output: false

all_transcripts <- rbind(sb_files, tv_show_df)

all_transcripts <- all_transcripts|>
  #renaming the second column to text as that is what is expected for the pybiber pipeline below
  rename(text = "clean_words",
         doc_id = "id")
```

Now we save this file to our private folder!

```{r}
write_csv(all_transcripts, "private/all_transcripts.csv")
```


## Summary all_transcripts

Below is some summary information about what is included in all_transcripts:

Number of rows and columns in our df and breakdown of genre

```{r}
nrow(all_transcripts)
ncol(all_transcripts)
all_transcripts |>
  mutate(doc_id = case_when(str_detect(doc_id, "trn") ~ "natural", 
                        str_detect(doc_id, "comedy") ~ "comedy", 
                        str_detect(doc_id, "drama") ~ "drama")) |>
  mutate(nwords = (str_count(text, "\\w+"))) |>
  count(doc_id)
```

Approximate number of words in our df:

```{r}
all_transcripts |>
  mutate(nwords = (str_count(text, "\\w+"))) |>
  summarize(sum(nwords))
```

Approximate number of words by category:

```{r}
all_transcripts |>
  mutate(doc_id = case_when(str_detect(doc_id, "trn") ~ "natural", 
                        str_detect(doc_id, "comedy") ~ "comedy", 
                        str_detect(doc_id, "drama") ~ "drama")) |>
  mutate(nwords = (str_count(text, "\\w+"))) |>
  group_by(doc_id) |>
  summarize(sum(nwords))
```

## Tagging all_transcripts and Getting Factor Loadings

In order to parse the data, it is necessary to use spaCy to tag all of the words in the document. Then, an r package called `pseudobibeR` can be used to get the 67 linguistic features created by Biber. For more details on the process, see [here](https://github.com/browndw/pseudobibeR). Note that this package and the following were created by David Brown, a linguist at CMU!

First, we can ensure that all texts are normalized and in a corpus format. A glimpse of the corpus format can be seen below.

```{r}
# 1. Read the texts and normalize typographic quotes (’ -> ')
all_transcripts$clean_words <- utf8::utf8_normalize(all_transcripts$clean_words, map_quote = TRUE)
corp <- corpus(all_transcripts)

corp
```
Next, we will download an English parsing model through `udpipe`. 

```{r}
# 2. Parse with udpipe (the model is downloaded once)
model <- udpipe_download_model(language = "english")
```

```{r}
ud_model <- udpipe_load_model(model$file_model)
```

And parse each character in the corpus. This process takes some time, around ten minutes. 

```{r}
parsed <- udpipe_annotate(ud_model, x = as.character(corp), doc_id = docnames(corp), trace = 100)
```

Finally, we can get the feature weights which will be used in the second half of functions. This function also takes some time to run, about five minutes. 

```{r}
# 3. Count the features: one row per document
features <- biber(parsed)
```


## Getting Dimension Scores

As can be seen in the features data structure, have feature loadings for each text. These can now be run through another series of functions to get the overall scores for the 67 linguistic features for each text. 

Once read in, the process described [here](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/mda.biber/vignettes/introduction.html) is used to run our first attempt at the MDA. 

Note that the documents are being renamed below such that each individual file is represented by it's category and no other information. For instance, each comedy TV show will only be known as comedy. This is necessary since we are comparing the groups as a whole.

```{r}
#| output: false

#ok so first we are assigning our data set to the variable d
d <- features |>
  #then, we are modifying a column called doc_id to rename columns that contain either "comedy", "drama" or "trn" with "comedy", "drama", and "natural". 
  mutate(doc_id = case_when(str_detect(doc_id, "comedy") ~ "comedy",
                            str_detect(doc_id, "drama") ~ "drama",
                            str_detect(doc_id, "trn") ~ "natural")) |>
  #then we are modifying our new column so the strings are factors
  mutate(doc_id = as.factor(doc_id)) |>
  #removes the columns with values = 0
  select(where(~ any(. != 0)))
```

This changes the labels of the id column so that our groups are formed, turns them into factors, and removes any columns with 0 instances. 

## Determining Ideal Number of Factors

The next step in the analysis is to decide on how many factors should be formed from the factor loadings. See the [MDA](mda.md) document for more details.

```{r}
screeplot_mda(d)
```
A screeplot displays 'eigenvalues'. Simply put, it groups feature weights based on their impact on the data. Large feature loadings will therefore be grouped together, medium feature loadings grouped together, and so on. 

The 'elbow' is essentially the cut off point where the features being grouped are not particularly impactful in terms of their predictive power. Visually, it is where the line becomes less steep. Anything at or below the elbow is considered 'scree'. In this case, based on the AF value, we can roughly mark that as the elbow. Since there are two points above that, we should include two factors 

```{r}
cor_m <- cor(d[,-1], method = "pearson")

corrplot(cor_m, type = "upper", order = "hclust", tl.col = "black", tl.srt = 45, diag = F, tl.cex = 0.5)
```
This plot is a representation of correlation between features. Blue indicates positive correlation along and red indicates negative correlation. So, we can see that a number of these features are correlated, so an MDA analysis makes sense. 

Here we are running the mda. Essentially, we are getting mean scores for the significan feature loadings within each dimension. 

```{r}
#now for the actual mda, factors is set equal to 2 because of the screeplot results
m <- mda_loadings(d, n_factors = 2)
```

And below we can see these mean values. 

```{r}
dimension_scores <- attributes(m)$group_means

dimension_scores
```

Immediately, we can see a substantial difference between Factor 1 and Factor 2. While Drama scores quite distinctly from the other two groups in Factor 1, Natural language is quite different along Factor 2. A deeper analysis of the differences between these two factors will likely lead to a better understanding of where dramaticity comes into play. 


```{r}
#values arranged in descending order for factor 1
attributes(m)$loadings |> arrange(Factor1)
```

```{r}
#values arranged in descending order for factor 1
attributes(m)$loadings |> arrange(-Factor2)
```

If we consider Drama TV shows to generally have language that is more exaggerated compared to comedy TV shows and real life, than we could posit that dimension 1 is more likely to reflect the dimension of dramaticity. It is likely that dimension 2, then, more reflects differences between natural discourse and tv show discourse that are shared between the drama and comedy genre. A further analysis of the specific features involved will likely support this.

Given this hypothysis, for now we will focus on dimension 1.

```{r}
#mapping the mean dimension scores centered around 0
stickplot_mda(m, n_factor = 1)
```
This graph is a useful tool for understanding what the dimension analysis is actually saying. Since scores are averaged around 0, it is very easy to see how the different groups are on opposite ends of the spectrum for this dimension. 


```{r}
heatmap_mda(m, n_factor = 1)
```

By including the relevant features, things become even clearer. One important reminder is that highly positive and highly negative features (such as mean word length and adverbs) are in a trade off relationship. Among these groups, as the mean length of a word increases we would expect fewer adverbs to be present and vice versa. 

Two immediate thoughts based on this graph:

- it is suprising that emphatics are less likely to occur in drama TV show transcripts

- it is surprising that adverbs are also so unlikely in drama TV show transcripts

It will be important to sample some of the tags for these documents to better understand what is causing these rates. What sorts of words are being tagged as adverbs so frequently in the SB files?

## Linear Mixed Effect Model

A good next step in the analysis is to determine whether these groupings are significantly different along their dimensions. To do so, lme4 can be used. 

## Considering Relevant Features

Assuming Dimension one is more fitting for dramaticity, relevant features that may have to do with Dramaticity based on these results:

High presense of:
-mean word length, prepositions, other nouns, nominalizations

Low presense of:
-adverbs, pronoun it, emphatics, present tense, proverb do
